input.vignette:
A 5-year-old female child is brought to a medical office with complaints of progressive abdominal pain that has intensified in the last 24 hours. The father reports a history of constipation, with no bowel movement for the past 72 hours and no bloody stools. She has experienced three episodes of vomiting since the previous night and is refusing food. Her medical and surgical history is unremarkable. Physical examination reveals upper abdominal distention with tympany, but no abdominal mass, involuntary guarding, or rebound tenderness is detected. What is the most probable underlying etiology of her clinical presentation?

Options:
A. Hirschsprung disease
B. Intestinal lymphoma
C. Superior mesenteric artery syndrome
D. Chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction
E. Volvulus
F. Malrotation of the gut
G. Pyloric stenosis
H. Intussusception
I. Meckel diverticulum
J. Duodenal web

The surgery was completed under spinal anesthesia, and a male neonate was delivered with a birthweight of 3.47 kg and a length of 51 cm. There were no complications during pregnancy, and all prenatal sonographic exams were normal. The newborn examination showed no dysmorphism. Post-C-section, the baby was transferred to the nursery for routine care and feeding. However, 24 hours post-delivery, the baby was moved to the neonatal intensive care unit due to poor feeding, bilious vomiting, and abdominal distension. Physical examination revealed normal vitals, persistent abdominal distension upon palpation, sluggish movements, and bloody mucoid stools. The baby was put under nil by mouth, and a nasogastric tube was inserted, revealing a light greenish aspirate. An x-ray showed multiple loops of dilated small bowel indicating obstruction. Intravenous fluids were started, and antibiotics (amoxicillin 50 mg every 12 hours and gentamicin 5 mg every 48 hours) were administered due to the possibility of bowel necrosis and perforation. The case was referred to pediatric surgery, and . Confirmed diagnosis: Hirschsprung’s disease. Differential diagnosis includes: Hirschsprung’s disease.

Entamoeba hiatolytica, which causes amoebic colitis, is another IBD mimicker that can cause bloody diarrhea. Endoscopic findings include skip lesions and multifocal ulceration, which is more common on the right side of the colon and can mimic CD. Microbiologically, the diagnosis of amoebiasis can be made by stool microscopy and periodic‐acid Schiff (PAS) positive trophozoites on biopsy. Histologically, there are flask‐shaped ulcers with florid necroinflammatory exudate, erythrophagocytosis, cryptitis, lamina propria‐containing chronic inflammatory infiltrates, surface epithelial damage, and PAS stains highlight the organisms. In contrast to IBD, the mucosa adjacent to the amoebic ulcers is normal, with an absence of granuloma. Of note, chronic amoebic infection can lead to crypt distortion and fibrosis, which could mimic IBD.

Presentation: Patient A, a 31-year-old woman, visited the hospital on 1 June 2017 due to 'fatigue and dizziness for 1 month and worsening for 1 week.' The patient experienced dizziness and fatigue without any clear cause 1 month prior, with symptoms intensifying over the past week. She sought care at the emergency department. Blood tests revealed a hemoglobin (HGB) level of 38 g/L, and esophagogastroduodenoscopy indicated chronic superficial gastritis. Despite blood replenishment treatment, severe anemia persisted, and symptoms of dizziness and fatigue showed minimal improvement. Consequently, the patient was admitted for 'anemia of unknown origin.' During her hospital stay, she did not report nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, abdominal distension, black stool, or bloody stool. Physical examination noted an anemic appearance, a soft abdomen without tenderness or rebound pain, no palpable masses, and bowel sounds occurring six times per minute. Admission findings included anemia of unknown origin. Blood tests showed HGB at 45 g/L; urine analysis revealed 94 RBC/μl; stool occult blood test was positive; and tumor marker tests indicated erythropoietin levels >762.00 mIU/ml. Contrast-enhanced CT sca. Confirmed diagnosis: Small Intestinal Lymphangioma. Differential diagnosis includes: Small Intestinal Lymphangioma.

Presentation: A 38-year-old male with a history of type III intestinal failure due to chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction related to gastrointestinal dysmotility, cardiac and intestinal arrhythmia syndrome, dependence on parenteral nutrition, sinus dysfunction, and a pacemaker. The patient has chronic intestinal insufficiency due to a motor disorder of the intestines and has been part of an intestinal rehabilitation program requiring regular monitoring of nutritional, biometric, and electrolytic parameters. The patient was admitted to a high-complexity hospital presenting with diffuse, mild-intensity abdominal pain for six days and multiple vomiting episodes. There was no fever, diarrhea, jaundice, or other associated symptoms. Vital signs upon admission were: blood pressure 98/54 mmHg, heart rate 67 per minute, respiratory rate 16 per minute, and oxygen saturation 95%. Physical examination showed an alert and oriented patient with mild dehydration, minimal tenderness upon abdominal palpation, and no clear signs of peritoneal irritation. A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan revealed intestinal obstruction with a transition zone in the jejunum, without signs of complications or intestinal loop. Confirmed diagnosis: Wernicke's Encephalopathy. Differential diagnosis includes: Wernicke's Encephalopathy.

Entamoeba hiatolytica, which causes amoebic colitis, is another IBD mimicker that can cause bloody diarrhea. Endoscopic findings include skip lesions and multifocal ulceration, which is more common on the right side of the colon and can mimic CD. Microbiologically, the diagnosis of amoebiasis can be made by stool microscopy and periodic‐acid Schiff (PAS) positive trophozoites on biopsy. Histologically, there are flask‐shaped ulcers with florid necroinflammatory exudate, erythrophagocytosis, cryptitis, lamina propria‐containing chronic inflammatory infiltrates, surface epithelial damage, and PAS stains highlight the organisms. In contrast to IBD, the mucosa adjacent to the amoebic ulcers is normal, with an absence of granuloma. Of note, chronic amoebic infection can lead to crypt distortion and fibrosis, which could mimic IBD.

Presentation: Patient A, a 31-year-old woman, visited the hospital on 1 June 2017 due to 'fatigue and dizziness for 1 month and worsening for 1 week.' The patient experienced dizziness and fatigue without any clear cause 1 month prior, with symptoms intensifying over the past week. She sought care at the emergency department. Blood tests revealed a hemoglobin (HGB) level of 38 g/L, and esophagogastroduodenoscopy indicated chronic superficial gastritis. Despite blood replenishment treatment, severe anemia persisted, and symptoms of dizziness and fatigue showed minimal improvement. Consequently, the patient was admitted for 'anemia of unknown origin.' During her hospital stay, she did not report nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, abdominal distension, black stool, or bloody stool. Physical examination noted an anemic appearance, a soft abdomen without tenderness or rebound pain, no palpable masses, and bowel sounds occurring six times per minute. Admission findings included anemia of unknown origin. Blood tests showed HGB at 45 g/L; urine analysis revealed 94 RBC/μl; stool occult blood test was positive; and tumor marker tests indicated erythropoietin levels >762.00 mIU/ml. Contrast-enhanced CT sca. Confirmed diagnosis: Small Intestinal Lymphangioma. Differential diagnosis includes: Small Intestinal Lymphangioma.

Presentation: A 38-year-old male with a history of type III intestinal failure due to chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction related to gastrointestinal dysmotility, cardiac and intestinal arrhythmia syndrome, dependence on parenteral nutrition, sinus dysfunction, and a pacemaker. The patient has chronic intestinal insufficiency due to a motor disorder of the intestines and has been part of an intestinal rehabilitation program requiring regular monitoring of nutritional, biometric, and electrolytic parameters. The patient was admitted to a high-complexity hospital presenting with diffuse, mild-intensity abdominal pain for six days and multiple vomiting episodes. There was no fever, diarrhea, jaundice, or other associated symptoms. Vital signs upon admission were: blood pressure 98/54 mmHg, heart rate 67 per minute, respiratory rate 16 per minute, and oxygen saturation 95%. Physical examination showed an alert and oriented patient with mild dehydration, minimal tenderness upon abdominal palpation, and no clear signs of peritoneal irritation. A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan revealed intestinal obstruction with a transition zone in the jejunum, without signs of complications or intestinal loop. Confirmed diagnosis: Wernicke's Encephalopathy. Differential diagnosis includes: Wernicke's Encephalopathy.
